papers.title_in_file: Quantum reservoir computing for photonic entanglement witnessing
papers.version_note: arXiv:2502.18361v2, 17 Dec 2025. The record id names the paper's GitHub repository (salvatore-lorenzo/arXiv-2502.18361-QELMWITNESS), which the paper cites for its data and code; the text is the paper itself.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental photonic quantum extreme learning machine (a memoryless quantum reservoir) that estimates entanglement witnesses of two-photon polarization states from single-setting orbital angular momentum measurements, benchmarked against shadow tomography.

assertions.value: The authors describe a QELM as a protocol in which input states pass through a fixed quantum channel (the reservoir) that disperses the information into a larger Hilbert space before measurement, and a linear readout layer trained on pre-characterized states recovers the target features from the measurement data.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Overview of QELMs, p.2
quotes: dispersing the information into a larger Hilbert space prior to measurement.
A linear readout layer is then trained on a set of pre-characterized states to recover the target features from the measurement data.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the QELM protocol in Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that the readout operator W is obtained by supervised training on a set of known training states, and that training solves a linear system for W; the states are assumed known, which the authors say amounts to a high degree of control of input state preparation.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Training, p.2
quotes: The operator W is obtained via a supervised training procedure using a set of known training states
one solves for W the linear system
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its training procedure in Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that the solvability of Eq. (1) is guaranteed provided the effective POVM is informationally complete, the training statistics are sufficiently large, and the training states span linearly the full state space.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Training, p.3
quotes: The solvability of Eq. (1) is guaranteed provided that the effective POVM
is informationally complete, the training statistics are sufficiently large, and the training states span linearly the full state space
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes this condition to its earlier QELM theory paper, citing it rather than proving it here.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the effective POVM symbol and the citation number in the same sentence; the sentence is split across two quotes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the linear regression problem for W is solved by the ordinary least squares estimator computed via the pseudoinverse, and that in their experiments the pseudoinverse method proved optimal.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Training, p.2-3
quotes: by the ordinary least squares estimator computed via the
In our experiments, the pseudoinverse method proved optimal, and we thus assume henceforth that W is computed via the pseudoinverse.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical statement about the authors' own experiments; no comparison data are shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that training a QELM produces a shadow estimator tailored to the specific apparatus without explicit knowledge of its internal workings, and that in the limit of large training statistics the linear operator W converges to the estimator employed in shadow tomography.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Connection with shadow tomography, p.3
quotes: training a QELM produces a shadow estimator tailored to the specific apparatus without requiring explicit knowledge of its internal workings
in the limit of large training statistics, the linear operator W converges to the estimator employed in shadow tomography
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the main text with citations to the earlier shadow tomography and QELM theory papers; not proved in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that QELMs exchange the need for a full characterization of the measurement apparatus, required in shadow tomography, for the simpler task of characterizing a restricted set of input states, and that this is advantageous when preparing input states accurately is easier than modeling the whole apparatus.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Connection with shadow tomography, p.3
quotes: QELMs exchange the need for a full characterization of the measurement apparatus
This shift is particularly advantageous when ac-
curately preparing the input states is easier than accurately modeling the entire experimental apparatus.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own argument for the method's niche, not tested against a case where state preparation is the harder part.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage is conditional on state preparation being easier to characterize than the apparatus; the paper does not measure a case where it is not.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as long as the target functionals are linear (such as expectation values of observables) and training uses linear regression, there is effectively no room for overfitting, and that insufficient training statistics instead produce a bias in the estimator.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A, Overfitting, p.13
quotes: As long as one restricts the target functionals to linear ones (e.g., expectation values of observables) and uses linear regression for training, there is effectively no room for overfitting.
If the training statistics are insufficient, however, the resulting estimator may carry a bias, leading to systematic estimation errors during testing
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative argument in the appendix; no overfitting test is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is scoped to linear targets; the paper does not claim it for nonlinear features.

assertions.value: The authors state that to reconstruct any observable at the testing stage the training states must span the space of all density matrices, so d squared random pure states are in principle sufficient to train a QELM (d the Hilbert space dimension), and that fewer training states can work if the test states lie in the span of the training ones.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A, Structure of training states, p.13
quotes: the training states must span the space of all density matrices.
Consequently, d2 random pure states are in principle sufficient to train a QELM.
The only requirement is that each testing density matrix can be in the linear span of the training ones.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof in this paper; the proof sits in the earlier QELM theory paper it cites. The exponent is printed flat in the text layer (d2 for d squared).

assertions.value: The authors state that the canonical solution for W can be written in terms of the canonical dual POVM of the effective measurement, so that training a QELM effectively recovers the dual of the underlying (effective) measurement.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A, Interpretability of the training process, p.12
quotes: Thus, training a QELM effectively recovers the dual of the underlying (effective) measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the relation to its earlier QELM theory paper and does not re-derive it.

assertions.value: The authors state that deviations of the finite-sample probability matrix from the true probability matrix lead to a biased estimator W, and thus to biased estimates for any target observable, and call this bias the counterpart for QELMs of the systematic errors from inaccurate apparatus modelization in other approaches.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A, Effects of finite statistics on the training, p.12
quotes: lead to a biased estimator W for the input state, and thus to biased estimates for any target observable.
This bias is the counterpart for QELMs of the systematic errors introduced
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative statement of a limitation; no derivation of the bias is given in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QELM test-stage estimate is an empirical mean over outcomes whose expectation is the true expectation value of the observable, and that its variance is inversely proportional to the number of test shots.
assertions.anchor: Appendix A, Effects of finite statistics on the test, p.13
quotes: while its variance Var[oˆNtest ] is inversely propor-
tional to Ntest.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the appendix without a derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote is split across a line break in the text layer.

assertions.value: The paper defines an entanglement witness as an observable whose expectation value is guaranteed to be non-negative for all separable states but negative for at least one entangled state, so that a negative expectation value certifies that the state is entangled.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Estimating entanglement witnesses, p.4
quotes: An entanglement witness W is an observable whose expectation value is guaranteed to be non-negative for all separable states, but negative for at least one entangled state
measuring Tr(Wρ) < 0 certifies that the state ρ is indeed entangled.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper's results depend on, stated in Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that, once trained on a set of states spanning the entire state space, the QELM can estimate arbitrary observables for new states, and that even a training set of only pure product states lets it capture entanglement features of unseen entangled states.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Estimating entanglement witnesses, p.4
quotes: Crucially, even if this training set consists only of pure product states, the QELM can still capture entanglement features of unseen entangled states
assertions.certainty_reason: Supported by the paper's experiments on one platform; the first remark of the effect is attributed to earlier work.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement holds in the paper only when the product-state training set spans the full state space; the rank analysis in Appendix B3 shows this fails for some configurations.

assertions.value: The authors describe the reservoir as two parallel discrete-time quantum walks, one per photon, in polarization and orbital angular momentum, built from waveplates and q-plates, whose output spans a 25-dimensional walker space (five OAM values per photon) that is then measured projectively in the OAM basis.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Reservoir dynamic and measurement, p.4
quotes: The resulting double QW evolution generates output states spanning a 25-dimensional walker space, given by the OAM values
this final projective OAM measurement results in a non-projective, single-setting, informationally-complete POVM on the twophoton input.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup in Section II.B.

assertions.value: The authors report that photon pairs are generated by spontaneous parametric down-conversion in a periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate crystal in a Sagnac configuration, and that adjusting the pump polarization switches between separable and maximally entangled states.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Input states preparation, p.4
quotes: By adjusting the pump polarization, we can switch between generating separable and maximally entangled states.
This architecture enables the generation of stable polarization-entangled states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report photon pairs at 808 nm produced by spontaneous parametric down-conversion in a periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate crystal in a Sagnac interferometer, pumped by a continuous-wave laser at 404 nm.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B2, Photon-pair generation, p.14
quotes: Photon pairs at 808 nm are produced via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC)
pumped by a continuous-wave laser at 404 nm and placed within a Sagnac interferometer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report three main experimental configurations: E1 uses waveplate angles numerically optimized to minimize the average reconstruction mean-squared error, E2 is derived from E1 by swapping two of the optimized angles, and E3 uses a fully random set of waveplate angles sampled uniformly.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Summary of experimental settings, p.4
quotes: E1 uses wave-plates angles that were numerically optimized to minimize the average reconstruction meansquared error (MSE)
E2 is derived from E1 by swapping two of the optimized angles, perturbing the reservoir dynamics.
E3 uses a fully random set of waveplate angles, sampled uniformly.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental settings.

assertions.value: The authors report that each configuration tests an equal number of separable and entangled states, 150 for E1 and E3 and 83 for E2, that the reference separable state is VV for E1 and VH for E2 and E3, and that the difference in statistics is due to experimental issues during data acquisition.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Summary of experimental settings, p.4
quotes: In each configurations we test an equal number of separable and entangled states, namely 150 for E1 and E3, and 83 for E2.
|ΨR⟩ = |V V ⟩ for E1 and |ΨR⟩ = |V H⟩ for E2 and E3.
is simply due to experimental issues during the data acquisition process
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup and sample sizes.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors expect the sample-size difference to have no significant impact; that is their expectation, not a tested result.

assertions.value: The authors report, for configuration E1 with training on both separable and entangled states, a training mean-squared error of about 0.009 and a test mean-squared error of about 0.017 for the entanglement witness expectation value, with 150 separable and 150 entangled states in each of the training and test sets.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Entanglement witness performance with mixed training, p.5-6, Fig. 3(a)
quotes: Figure 3 reports the results for the E1 configuration, in which training and testing use two sets, each comprising 150 separable and 150 entangled states.
MSEtrain ≃ 0.009 for training, MSEtest ≃ 0.017 for testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experimental run of one configuration.

assertions.value: The authors report that in E1 with mixed training, entanglement is correctly certified for 91.4% of the entangled states with a negative witness value, and that with a threshold of three standard deviations (square root of the training mean-squared error) 37.1% of entangled states remain certifiably entangled.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Entanglement witness performance with mixed training, p.6, Fig. 3(c)
quotes: entanglement is correctly certified for 91.4% of these states.
we find that 37.1% of entangled states remain certifiably entangled even within this elevated error tolerance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experimental dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that averaging over random training instances in E1 gives a training mean-squared error of 0.010 plus or minus 0.001, a test mean-squared error of 0.015 plus or minus 0.001, and (89 plus or minus 4)% certified entangled states, with errors being one standard deviation.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Entanglement witness performance with mixed training, p.6
quotes: MSEtrain = 0.010 ± 0.001 and MSEtest = 0.015 ± 0.001, with a number of certified entangled states equal to (89 ± 4)%.
The reported errors represent one standard deviation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experimental dataset resampled over training subsets.

assertions.value: The authors report that in E1, training on all 150 separable states and testing on all 150 entangled states gives a training mean-squared error of about 0.004 and a test mean-squared error of about 0.04, with 73.7% of entangled states correctly certified and 32.9% certified within three standard deviations.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Generalization performances, p.6, Fig. 3(b), 3(d)
quotes: when the training dataset contains all 150 separable states, while the test dataset contains all 150 entangled ones.
The training and test MSEs are MSEtrain ≃ 0.004 and MSEtest ≃ 0.04.
is 73.7%. Accounting for stochastic errors, 32.9% of entangled states remain certified within three standard deviations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experimental dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: Certification falls from 91.4% (mixed training) to 73.7% (separable-only training) in the same configuration, so out-of-distribution training costs accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because separable states alone span the space of all states, a QELM trained only on separable states can still perform well on previously unseen entangled states, though the model was never trained on any state with a negative witness value.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Generalization performances, p.6
quotes: because separable states alone span the space of all states, it follows that a QELM can be trained exclusively on separable states yet still perform well on previously unseen entangled states.
assertions.certainty_reason: A reasoned statement supported by one experimental result; the rank analysis in Appendix B3 shows the span condition fails for some configurations.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement holds only where the separable training states actually span the test states; see the E2, E3, E5 and E6 rank results.

assertions.value: The authors report that when the entangled reference state is replaced by mixtures of the form (1 minus p) times the entangled state plus p times the separable state, but labeled with the value for the maximally entangled state, in configuration E2 the performance remains robust for noise levels up to p = 0.5.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Effect of input states mislabeling, p.6-7, Fig. 4(a,b)
quotes: ρnoise = (1 − p)ρent + pρsep
with performance remaining robust for noise levels up to p = 0.5.
The study was performed in the experimental scenario E2
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one configuration; the mixed states are built numerically from measured OAM distributions, not prepared in the lab.
assertions.reader_inference: The mixtures are constructed by weighting measured distributions, so this tests robustness to mislabeled training data rather than to a physical noise channel.

assertions.value: The authors state that the noise dataset was built by taking a weighted combination of the experimentally measured OAM distributions for entangled and separable states.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Effect of input states mislabeling, p.6
quotes: by taking a weighted combination of the experimentally measured OAM distributions for entangled and separable states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of how its noise dataset was built.

assertions.value: The authors report, from numerical simulations, that the average mean-squared error is inversely proportional to the number of collected samples N after an initial settling regime, with the test mean-squared error decreasing as beta over N, beta being a constant that depends on the measurement setting; until the estimator is sufficiently unbiased, the error decreases at a slower rate.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Dependence of performances on reservoir configuration, p.7, Fig. 4(c)
quotes: we still observe, at least in numerical simulations, the expected inverse proportionality between the average MSE and the number of collected samples N
the test MSE decreases as β/N , with β a proportionality constant that depends on the specifics of the measurement setting.
until the estimator W is sufficiently unbiased, the MSE decreases at a slower rate than 1/N .
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation result of this paper's configurations, not a proved bound.

assertions.value: The authors report that different reservoir configurations yield different estimation accuracies under the same training statistics, because they correspond to different effective POVMs, and that the E1 angles reach the inverse-N regime with the available experimental statistics while E2 and E3 require additional statistics.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Dependence of performances on reservoir configuration, p.7, Fig. 4(c)
quotes: different reservoir configurations can yield different estimation accuracies under the same training statistics.
In contrast, the configurations E2 and E3 require additional statistics before reaching the same performance level.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical and simulated results for three configurations.

assertions.value: The authors state that the acquisition time was set so a full data acquisition completes within 10 hours, giving an average overall signal of about 3000 coincidence counts per state; the appendix separately reports an average of 1117 plus or minus 76 counts per state over all 25 outcomes for E1.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B p.7 and Appendix B2, Estimated experimental statistics, p.15
quotes: within 10 hours having an average overall signal of ∼ 3000 coincidence counts per state.
The overall average counts per state is then found to be 1117 ± 76 cc/state, summing the observed counts over all 25 outcomes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Two experimental figures from the paper; they differ.
assertions.reader_inference: The main text (about 3000) and the appendix (1117 for E1) differ; the main-text figure may refer to a different configuration or to counts before polarization projection. The paper does not reconcile them.

assertions.value: The authors report an estimated coincidence rate of about 6.1 Hz for each output event, computed from measured element efficiencies, against an observed rate of about 2.9 Hz in E1; acquisition was 8 seconds per projection, repeated 2 times.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B2, Estimated experimental statistics, p.15
quotes: ccteo = ηQ2 Wηp2rojηS2LMηS2MFccs ≈ 6.1 Hz.
By comparison, for the E1 experimental configuration we observed a rate of ≈ 2.9 Hz.
we set the acquisition time to 8 seconds per projection, then, repeating each measurement 2 times
assertions.certainty_reason: Experimental measurements and an efficiency-based estimate from one setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The observed rate is below half the estimate; the paper does not explain the gap.

assertions.value: The authors report a pump power of about 8 mW, a source coincidence rate of about 20 kHz, and measured efficiencies of about 0.80 for the q-plates, 0.56 for the whole quantum walk, 0.5 per photon for the polarization projection, 0.78 for the spatial light modulator and 0.4 for the single-mode fiber coupling.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B2, Estimated experimental statistics, p.15
quotes: having a power P ≈ 8 mW, and yielding a coincidence rate of ccs ≈ 20 kHz
we obtained efficiencies ηQP ≈ 0.80 and ηQW ≈ 0.56, respectively.
ηproj ≈ 0.5 per photon
ηSLM ≈ 0.78 and ηSMF ≈ 0.4, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured hardware figures from one setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The total optical efficiency is low, which is why the paper's counts per state are small.

assertions.value: The authors report, for E1 and the witness of the Phi plus state, a shadow tomography mean-squared error of about 0.015 for separable and 0.072 for entangled states, against 0.002 and 0.041 for a QELM trained solely on separable states and 0.009 and 0.017 for a QELM trained on both.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Benchmark with shadow tomography, p.7-8; Table S3, p.23
quotes: shadow tomography yields an MSE of approximately 0.015 for separable states and 0.072 for entangled states.
In contrast our QELM, trained solely on separable states, reduces these MSEs to 0.002 and 0.041, respectively.
Doing the training on both separable and entangled states gives the even smaller MSEs 0.009 and 0.017.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical comparison on one configuration and one witness.
assertions.reader_inference: A single configuration and a single witness; the shadow tomography figures use the best unknown-N guess per observable, so they are favorable to shadow tomography.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reported shadow-tomography errors are lower bounds, because shadow tomography needs the input statistics N, which is unavailable, so they report the minimum over guessed N values, and that this minimum depends on the target observable and is therefore not a physical estimate of the true N.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B p.7 and Appendix D, Knowing counts vs frequencies, p.22
quotes: the reported shadow-tomography MSEs represent lower bounds
we instead report the MSE as a function of the guessed N and then take its minimum value.
the values obtained should be viewed as lower bounds on what would be achieved if the true N were known.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of the scope and bias of its own benchmark in Appendix D.
assertions.reader_inference: The benchmark compares a trained estimator with a model-based one using a best-case unknown-N setting; this favors shadow tomography.

assertions.value: The authors state that in principle one could build a much more detailed physical model of the apparatus and push the shadow-tomography performance beyond that of the QELM, but that building and validating such a model is time-consuming and resource-intensive.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Benchmark with shadow tomography, p.7
quotes: In principle, one could build a much more detailed physical model of the apparatus and, with it, push the shadow-tomography performance beyond that of the QELM.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own benchmark in Section II.B.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported QELM advantage is therefore against a shadow tomography estimator built from the ideal model, not against a calibrated model of the real apparatus.

assertions.value: The authors state that shadow tomography, like state tomography, requires no training dataset but needs explicit and accurate knowledge of the entire measurement apparatus, and that QELMs instead use a training dataset of states and their measurement outcomes.
assertions.anchor: Appendix D, How does shadow tomography work, p.22
quotes: requires no training dataset but instead demands explicit and accurate knowledge of the entire measurement apparatus.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of a method from the cited literature.

assertions.value: The authors state that the effective POVM used for shadow tomography is computed from the ideal isometry of the two quantum walks and the polarization projection state, and that the actual apparatus deviates from this idealized model owing to imperfections and thermal fluctuations.
assertions.anchor: Appendix D p.22 and Section II.A p.4
quotes: Owing to imperfections and thermal fluctuations, the actual apparatus deviates from this idealized model.
The corresponding effective POVM is given by
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own benchmark setup and the apparatus's deviation from the model.
assertions.reader_inference: The second quote is split across a page-layout break in the text layer; the formula that follows it is not quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that the shadow-tomography estimates across the board yield mean-squared errors significantly higher than those of the QELM, across configurations E1 to E4 and the four Bell witnesses, with the shadow-tomography mean-squared error shown against the unknown input statistics in Fig. S8.
assertions.anchor: Appendix D, Performances of theoretical model of the apparatus, p.22-23, Fig. S8
quotes: We find the shadow-tomography-based estimates to across the board
yield MSEs significantly higher than those given via the QELM.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical comparison; the per-configuration QELM errors for E2 to E4 are in the repository, not in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives side-by-side numbers only for E1 and the Phi plus witness (Table S3).

assertions.value: The authors state that QELMs do not require explicit knowledge of the total input count, because as long as the overall count rate remains sufficiently stable the QELM learns the appropriate scaling factor from raw counts, and that normalizing counts makes training and testing consistent when run at different statistics.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B1, Post-selection measurements, p.13
quotes: QELMs do not require explicit knowledge of the total input count;
as long as the overall count rate remains sufficiently stable, the QELM automatically learns the appropriate scaling factor
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative statement supported by the paper's experiments, which run at comparable training and test statistics.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself says training and test statistics were comparable, so the case of different statistics is argued but not tested.

assertions.value: The authors report that in their experiments training and test statistics are comparable and they do not observe a substantial difference in the results obtained with and without normalizing experimental counts.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B1, QELM training with counts vs frequencies, p.13-14
quotes: we thus do not observe a substantial difference in the results obtained with and without normalizing experimental counts.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical statement without data shown in the paper text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the polarization projection before the OAM measurement is needed because spatial light modulators only operate on photons with a fixed polarization, so the mapping from input density matrices to output probabilities is a non-trace-increasing completely positive map followed by a projective measurement, not strictly a channel followed by a POVM, which increases the data required for training and testing.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B1, Polarization projection, p.13
quotes: Our apparatus requires a polarization projection before OAM measurement because spatial light modulators only operate on photons with a fixed polarization
it can be modeled as a non-trace-increasing completely positive map, followed by a projective measurement.
just increases the amount of data (statistics) required for both training and testing
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of how its apparatus departs from the basic model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the setup projects sequentially onto each OAM state with a spatial light modulator and single-mode fiber, rather than performing a direct projective measurement, and that they find the resulting difference in statistics negligible in practice.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B1, Implementation of projective OAM measurement, p.14
quotes: we sequentially project onto each OAM state by using an SLM
we find that in practice this difference is negligible.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement supported by a Poisson approximation argument; no test is reported.

assertions.value: The authors report from full state tomography with maximum likelihood that the maximally entangled reference state has fidelity 0.923 plus or minus 0.002 and a CHSH parameter S of 2.685 plus or minus 0.013, with errors computed assuming Poissonian counts.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B2, Table S1, p.15
quotes: The errors are computed by assuming a Poissonian statistics on the experimentally measured counts.
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result for one prepared state; the table is read from the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The CHSH value exceeds 2, so the source state violates the CHSH inequality; the paper's training and test labels still treat the prepared entangled states as maximally entangled.

assertions.value: The authors report fidelity 0.905 plus or minus 0.002 and CHSH parameter 2.432 plus or minus 0.013 for the first partially entangled reference state, and fidelity 0.927 plus or minus 0.001 and CHSH parameter 2.301 plus or minus 0.012 for the second.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B2, Table S1, p.15
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured results for two prepared states; the table is read from the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that input states are generated by applying local unitaries, a quarter-wave plate after a half-wave plate on each photon, to the reference states with uniformly random angles, either the same angles on both photons (E1, E2, E3, E5, E6) or independently sampled angles (E4).
assertions.anchor: Appendix B3, Input states, p.15-16
quotes: In all cases, we generated the input states sampling uniformly random angles for each of the waveplates.
This is the scenario considered in the datasets E1, E2, E3, E5, E6.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that a rank of 16 for the separable training states means they span the entire 16-dimensional space of density matrices in their setup, so the QELM can learn any feature of any state, and that where the separable rank is below the rank of all states (E2, E3, E5, E6) some entangled states must be added to the training.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B3, Singular values and model trainability, p.16; Table S2, p.17
quotes: rank(M sep) = 16 means that the training separable states span the entire 16-dimensional space of density matrices in our setup
which happens for E2, E3, E5, E6, certain features of the test states lie outside the linear span of separable states, requiring to add some entangled states in the training.
assertions.certainty_reason: A rank analysis of this paper's datasets; the ranks are tabulated in Table S2 (9-9-9 for E1; 9-6-10 for E2, E3, E5, E6; 16-10-16 for E4).
assertions.reader_inference: The text and Table S2 disagree in form: the quote speaks of a rank of 16 for the span, while Table S2 lists a rank of 9 for the separable states in E1; the paper does not reconcile these in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that a higher separable-state rank corresponds to a higher resource requirement in training statistics per state, and that the best configuration depends on balancing these resource demands against the application.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B3, Singular values and model trainability, p.16
quotes: higher rank(M sep) corresponds to a higher resource requirement in terms of training statistics used per state.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of a trade-off, not tested separately.

assertions.value: The authors state that small singular values of the probability matrix correspond to observables that require large training statistics for accurate reconstruction, and that in E3 even N = 105 (printed flat; ten to the fifth) is insufficient to reproduce the smallest two singular values.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Singular values of counts matrices, p.16; Fig. S2 caption, p.17
quotes: small singular values correspond to observables that require large training statistics for accurate reconstruction.
In E3, for instance, even N = 105 is insufficient to reproduce the smallest two singular
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation and data result for this paper's configurations. The exponent is printed flat in the text layer (105 for ten to the five).

assertions.value: The authors report that with the VH reference separable state, the rank of all states exceeds the rank of the separable states, so entangled test states have a component the training never saw, producing a constant shift between true and predicted witness values even in the infinite-statistics simulation, and that adding just one entangled state to the training set fixes the bias.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Training with different reference separable states, p.18; Fig. S6, p.21
quotes: we have rank(M all) > rank(M sep), indicating that some test entangled states span directions the QELM never had a chance to learn about during training.
adding even just one single entangled state to the training dataset is sufficient to characterize that missing dimension, and thus fix the bias.
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation and experimental result for the E5 and E1 datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: This qualifies the paper's headline claim that separable-only training generalizes to entangled states: it fails for the VH reference state with equal preparation angles.

assertions.value: The authors state that the missing-direction bias does not arise when the reference separable state is VV, owing to the different symmetry properties of the reservoir in that case, and that how training states are generated can be crucial when the reservoir dynamics have specific symmetries.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Training with different reference separable states, p.19; Fig. S6
quotes: this issue does not arise when the reference separable state is |V V ⟩, owing to the different symmetry properties of the reservoir in this case.
the way training states are generated can be crucial from an estimation perspective
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical and simulated result for E1.

assertions.value: The authors state that in E1, with training on separable states and testing on maximally entangled states, the estimation mean-squared error depends on the choice of target observable, that local Pauli observables are easier to reconstruct with separable states, and that for local Pauli observables the maximally entangled test states have zero expectation value.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Additional data for E1, p.16; Fig. S3 caption, p.18
quotes: We observe that local observables are predictably easier to reconstruct when using separable states.
These results clearly show that the estimation MSE depends on the choice of target observable, in agreement with theoretical expectations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result for one configuration.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results for the Phi minus witness in E1 are trivial because of the symmetry of the generated states, which all give the same value for that witness.
assertions.anchor: Fig. S4 caption, Appendix C, p.19
quotes: The trivial results for the Φ− witness are due to the particular symmetry of states generated in the E1 configuration
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation for one configuration.
assertions.reader_inference: One of the four Bell witnesses reported in E1 gives a degenerate test, so the four-witness results are not four independent tests.

assertions.value: The authors report that in E4, where the input waveplate angles for the two quantum walks are chosen independently, the mean-squared errors are 0.021 for training and 0.022 for testing, that performance is somewhat lower than in E1, and that they attribute the reduction to the higher training-statistics requirement rather than a fundamental limitation.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Training with asymmetric input states, p.17; Fig. S5 caption, p.20
quotes: This dataset achieves values of the MSE equal to 0.021 and 0.022, respectively for the training and test set
though the performance is somewhat lower than in E1.
rather than from any fundamental limitation of the method.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result for one configuration; the attribution to training statistics is the authors' interpretation.
assertions.reader_inference: The attribution to training statistics is stated but, in the text, tested only by the claim that more data would recover E1 performance.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulation that estimation accuracy in retrieving negative witness values tends to decrease as the angle mismatch between the two input stages grows, with a smaller effect at higher statistics (125, 250 and 1250 signals), and that fewer generated states have negative witness values as the mismatch grows.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Fig. S5 caption, p.20
quotes: The results highlight that the estimation accuracy tends to decrease when δ increases, with a contribution that is less relevant for higher statistics.
for three different statistics conditions (125, 250, 1250 signals)
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation result averaged over 5000 mismatch draws.

assertions.value: The authors report that when partially entangled states are deliberately mislabeled as maximally entangled in a training set that is 50% of the dataset, the model keeps high accuracy across all three classes of entangled states, even for those with a negative witness value, and conclude that robust estimation can be maintained when undetected imperfections reduce the entanglement.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Training with partially entangled reference states, p.19; Fig. S7
quotes: We use a training dataset comprising 50% of the total dataset and intentionally mislabel the partially entangled states as maximally entangled.
the accuracy remains high across all three classes of entangled states, even for those with ⟨WΦ+ ⟩ < 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from two datasets, averaged over many random splits.
assertions.reader_inference: The accuracy figures are in Fig. S7, which the text layer does not carry as numbers.

assertions.value: The authors report datasets of 249 states for the first partially entangled reference state and 357 for the second, each equally divided among maximally entangled, partially entangled and separable states, generated with the R2 reservoir configuration and identical angles at the state preparation stage.
assertions.anchor: Appendix C, Training with partially entangled reference states, p.19
quotes: we collected a dataset of 249 states in the first case and 357 in the second
both equally divided among maximally entangled, partially entangled, and separable states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own dataset sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the training states are assumed known, which amounts to assuming a high degree of control of the input state preparation stage, and that imperfections in state preparation result in imperfections in the estimation.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Training, p.2; Appendix A, Advantages over alternative methods, p.12
quotes: Imperfections in state prepara-
tion will result in imperfections in the estimation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of the method in Section II.A.
assertions.reader_inference: The method moves the calibration burden to the state-preparation stage; the paper's own source was characterized by tomography with fidelity about 0.9 (Table S1).

assertions.value: The authors state that the apparatus is not expected to be ideal for state reconstruction, since its effective measurement differs substantially from the symmetric measurements, such as MUBs and SIC-POVMs, known to be optimal for such tasks, and that accurately modeling all its components and noise sources is challenging.
assertions.anchor: Section I, Introduction, p.1
quotes: This apparatus is not expected to be ideal for state reconstruction, since its effective measurement differs substantially from the symmetric measurements
accurately modeling all components of the apparatus and its noise sources is challenging.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own apparatus in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that E2 and E3 would need more statistics to reach the target regime, which could in principle be achieved by longer acquisition and more coincidence counts per state.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, Dependence of performances on reservoir configuration, p.7
quotes: In principle, this regime could be achieved experimentally by increasing the data acquisition time and, therefore, the number of coincidence counts for each state.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: The 1/N regime for E2 and E3 is shown only in simulation; the experiments did not reach it.

assertions.value: The authors claim, to the best of their knowledge, the first experimental implementation of a single-setting state-estimation architecture that is model-independent and allows witnessing nonclassical features of input states, and a step beyond earlier reconstructions of single-qubit properties.
assertions.anchor: Section I, Introduction, p.2
quotes: the first experimental implementation of a single-setting state-estimation architecture that is model-independent and allows to witness nonclassical features of input states
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim by the authors; not checked against the literature here.
assertions.reader_inference: Priority claims depend on a literature search the paper does not document.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that their approach does not require fine-tuning or refined knowledge of the setup, at the same time outperforming conventional approaches, and that it automatically adapts to noise and imperfections while avoiding overfitting.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1
quotes: Our approach does not require fine-tuning or refined knowledge of the setup, at the same time outperforming conventional approaches.
It automatically adapts to noise and imperfections while avoiding overfitting
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract-level claim; the supporting comparison is only against shadow tomography from the ideal model on this one apparatus.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison covers one conventional method on one hardware setup, with the shadow-tomography values given as lower bounds.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QELM eliminates the need for prior modeling of the measurement apparatus, thereby completely circumventing the challenges associated with fine-tuning and calibration, and that its linear supervised framework sidesteps the interpretability and overfitting issues of more complex architectures.
assertions.anchor: Section I, Introduction, p.2
quotes: it eliminates the need for prior modeling of the measurement apparatus, thereby completely circumventing the challenges associated with fine-tuning and calibration
it sidesteps the interpretability and overfitting issues often encountered with more complex architectures.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim of advantage; the training states still require calibrated preparation.
assertions.reader_inference: The method replaces apparatus modeling by state-preparation characterization, so calibration is moved to the source rather than removed (the paper says so in its own limit on training states being known).

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they experimentally demonstrated that a QELM can reconstruct an entanglement witness for bipartite two-photon states with performance on par with methods that rely on careful calibration and prior knowledge of the apparatus, and that the approach is platform-independent.
assertions.anchor: Section III, Discussion, p.7
quotes: achieving performance on par with methods that rely on careful calibration and prior knowledge of the apparatus.
our approach is platform-independent
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; platform independence is argued, not tested on a second platform.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments cover one photonic platform; the cross-platform claim is a projection.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that training solely on separable states is sufficient to accurately witness the entanglement of new, previously unseen input states, that the QELM self-calibrates to the experiment, and that drifts in the experimental setup can leave the final witness reconstruction largely unaffected.
assertions.anchor: Section III, Discussion, p.8
quotes: training solely on separable states is sufficient to accurately witness the entanglement of new, previously unseen input states
drifts in the experimental setup can leave the final witness reconstruction largely unaffected
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; the data show 73.7% certification for separable-only training in E1 and a failure mode for the VH reference state.
assertions.reader_inference: The Discussion's word 'sufficient' is stronger than the paper's own data: separable-only training certified 73.7% of entangled states in E1, and a constant bias appeared for the VH reference state in Appendix C. The drift claim is not tied to a measurement in the main text.

assertions.value: The authors state as a prospect that QELMs trained on fully classical data, for example coherent states, could later be applied to certify nonclassical properties of unknown quantum states with no additional overhead.
assertions.anchor: Section III, Discussion, p.8
quotes: transfer learning demonstrations, where QELMs trained on fully classical data (e.g. coherent-states) can later be applied to certify nonclassical properties of unknown quantum states
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated prospect with no data in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reservoir configuration values, the experimental data used to train and test the QELM in each configuration and the code used to generate the reported data are available in a GitHub repository, and that all data needed to evaluate the conclusions will be available in Zenodo.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B3, Experimental settings, p.15; Section V.D, p.9
quotes: is available at https://github.com/salvatore-lorenzo/arXiv-2502.18361-QELMWITNESS.
All data needed to evaluate the conclusions in the paper will be available in Zenodo.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of where its data and code are held.
assertions.reader_inference: The Zenodo statement is in the future tense; the paper does not give a Zenodo identifier.

assertions.value: The authors state that each quantum walk implements a two-step evolution, so the overall unitary is the tensor product of the two walks, that each photon ends in a superposition of five OAM states, giving a total 25-dimensional output walker space, and that the q-plate axis angles are fixed by the fabrication process.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Materials and Methods, p.8-9
quotes: we implement a two-step evolution in each of the two QWs
each photon is in a superposition of the five OAM states
leading to a total 25-dimensional output walker space.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that machine learning based state estimation methods are often deficient in interpretability, that the opacity of the underlying models can complicate assessing the reliability of their results, and that these issues are exacerbated when the goal is witnessing nonclassical features such as entanglement.
assertions.anchor: Section I, Introduction, p.1-2
quotes: ML-based methods, however, are often deficient in interpretability
These issues are further exacerbated when the goal is witnessing nonclassical features of quantum states, such as entanglement
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivating statement about other work, citing the literature without a comparison in this paper.
